newsitem.title: GERMANY: German steel merger talks begin amid protests.
newsitem.headline: German steel merger talks begin amid protests.

text.p: The bosses of Germany's two largest steel groups began talks on a merger of their steel operations on Thursday as workers downed tools in protest against a move which will cost thousands of jobs.

The talks are an attempt to avert a hostile takeover bid launched this week by Fried. Krupp AG Krupp-Hoesch against its larger rival Thyssen AG which rocked the consensual relationship among Germany's corporate, financial and political elite.

Thyssen chief executive Dieter Vogel and Krupp boss Gerhard Cromme met at a secret location to begin eight days of talks intended to merge their steel operations into a single unit which would rank among Europe's top three steel producers.

Krupp has said that if it cannot achieve an agreement, it will resurrect its takover offer, which relies on banks to finance an offer of 435 marks per Thyssen share, a 20 percent premium over Monday's closing price before the shares were suspended.

Wolfgang Clement, the state economics minister of North Rhine-Westphalia, which is home to most of Germany's coal and steel industry, told the state assembly in an emergency debate that some rationalisation was inevitable.
But he said there was now a chance to develop a German steel concept which could survive in the long term.

North Rhine-Westphalia put huge pressure on Krupp and Thyssen to try to find an alternative solution which would safeguard jobs and not abandon Germany's long tradition of consensus solutions in industry.
German unemployment is at its highest level since 1933.

State finance minister Heinz Schleusser told the Koelnische Rundschau daily that he was "cautiously optimistic that the talks can lead to a result that will again emphasise cooperation between the two firms".

Workers at both Krupp and Thyssen began a third day of protest stoppages -- a tactic which has helped to mobilise public opinion against a deal seen as having been agreed in backrooms between Krupp and its bankers, led by Deutsche Bank.

Krupp's steel production operations were run down to emergency levels as workers marched to a meeting in Dortmund, and production at Thyssen's Duisburg steelworks was also hit as about 1,000 workers downed tools to join the meeting in a show of solidarity.

Personnel director Juergen Rossberg sought to cool tempers by pledging that Krupp's Dortmund works, seen as the first to go in any rationalisation of the two companies' output, would not bear the brunt of restructuring alone.
Shares in both companies were suspended on Tuesday and Wednesday but resumed bourse trading on Thursday.

Thyssen closed at 375.80 marks compared with their March 17 after-hours close of 344.50, still well below Krupp's announced offer. Krupp stock closed at 313 marks against 270 marks on Monday, while the overall DAX index of leading German shares fell 1.55 percent.
Steel workers, trade unions and some politicians continued their attacks on Krupp's advances.
Walter Riester, deputy president of the IG Metall metal workers' union, attacked Krupp and Deutsche Bank for attempting a hostile takeover.
"With these Wild West methods they are trying to establish conditions that are common in America. But that is a different economic and social system," Riester said.

Schleusser, too, criticised Deutsche Bank for what he saw as its dubious role. "It is certainly alienating that bank representatives sit on the supervisory board of Thyssen on the one hand, and on the other hand are working on strategies that are directed against the company," he said.
But Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Federation of German Industry (BDI), dismissed what he called the partially hysterical attacks on Krupp.
"Mergers are normal," he said. "We have to get used to takeovers; they could make sense."
"This will lead to a greater competitiveness of the German steel industry," he added, noting that the concentration of the sector in France and Britain had brought large cost advantages.
